rv.q: It’s also a party with a great host and an open invitation, a kingdom in which we’re all welcome.
By Act II, Yee has hilariously thrown the conventions of the stage family story, even a self-referential one, out the window.
It’s an entertaining, shape-shifting romp among cultural themes from the author of Cambodian Rock Band and Mother Russia .
What better way to honor your complicated family–even as fictional Lauren prepares to move farther away from them–than to write them such a warm and witty tribute?
King of the Yees is both more moving than Cambodian Rock Band and funnier than this spring's dull-edged satire Mother Russia.
King of the Yees is an acclaimed family comedy and epic about finding your way through your lineage to discover your true self.

But if there is a serious intent detectable in the “King of the Yees,” and some genuinely warm and poignant moments, they are upstaged not just by Lauren’s fanciful adventures, but by an overeager display of metatheatrical noodling.

The metatheatrical moment is a surprisingly clunky start from the otherwise reliable Yee, who usually plunges her audiences right into the action, whether it’s for laughs ( Mother Russia ) or punches to the gut ( Cambodian Rock Band ).

Although 'King of the Yees' may not be a perfect way to continue the Yee legacy, it's a step forward, a resolute attempt to encapsulate the vibrant streets of Chinatown and ensure the story of all Yees everywhere continues to be told.
There are also a good many lulls between the jokes, and sequences that seem more clever in conception than execution.

cn.t: Yee's inventive meta-theatrical comedy about family and Chinese American identity earns praise for its playful structure and ambition, though some find its wacky, pop culture-fueled style more dazzling than coherent.
